summary: The note surveys folklore about death omens and ancestral spirits across ancient Mesopotamia, Greece, Europe, Africa, Asia, and indigenous cultures, citing scholars who spoke at 2023-2024 events. It also covers the revival of omen beliefs in contemporary culture and how ancestral spirit veneration was absorbed into religions such as Christianity and Islam. It concludes that these beliefs reflect a universal human quest to understand the unknown and seek guidance from the dead.
one_line: A cross-cultural survey of death omens and ancestral spirit beliefs, from ancient Mesopotamia to modern urban legends and religious traditions.
key_facts: Dr. Helena Marquez of the University of Barcelona said on October 12, 2023 that owls or ravens were interpreted in Mesopotamian cultures as warnings of impending doom.
Inscriptions from 2500 B.C.E. in the ruins of Ur describe a lone owl perched near a house as a sign that a family member was marked for the netherworld.
In ancient Greece, unexplained fires, ghostly apparitions, and sudden withering of crops were seen as portents of death.
Sarah Jennings of Oxford University said on November 3, 2023 that a common European belief held that a sudden unexplained drop in temperature signaled the approach of the Grim Reaper.
In English folklore, a sudden inexplicable ringing bell was thought an omen of imminent passing, while the Irish believed a banshee's wail means a family member will soon die.
At a September 20th, 2023 conference in Nairobi, the Luo community's belief was cited that seeing one's shadow without a head during sunset presages the observer's death.
Zulu folklore in South Africa holds that a night visit by an owl is a bad omen, sending messages from ancestors or indicating misfortune.
Dr. Feng Hsu said on December 17, 2023 that in Chinese culture a clock stopping suddenly can signal that someone in the household will die soon, and a sorrowfully howling dog signals a nearby death.

Psychologist Javier Mendoza of Buenos Aires attributed the revival of death omens, at a February 1, 2024 webinar, to increased stress and search for meaning during public health crises and natural disasters.
Modern omens include receiving a call from an unknown number that only produces static, spread via social media as new urban legends.
Dia de Los Muertos on November 2, 2023 honors the dead and invokes their blessings, with roots in ancient Aztec customs.
Among the Igbo people of Nigeria, ancestors are consulted for important events and their displeasure is thought to cause personal or communal misfortune.
Elder James White Elk of the Lakota Sioux said on September 10, 2023 that ancestral spirits are integral to every aspect of life, from the hunt to personal loss.
In the highlands of Papua New Guinea, clan spirit-houses serve as altars to commune with forebears and as repositories of their wisdom and protection.
Father Richard Evans, interviewed January 9, 2024, said saints are prayed to for intercession, similar to asking blessings from an ancestral spirit; All Saints' Day honors known and unknown saints.
